title: EUR 55,000 returned, and the team treated it as a cancellation. It was a payment in reverse.
explain:
EUR 55,000 settles to the wrong beneficiary.
A pacs.004 comes back through the chain.
The team files it as a cancellation, with no charges, no references and no controls.

Here is how that happens:

→ EUR 55,000 settles to the wrong beneficiary
→ pacs.004 return sent in reverse
→ Return filed as a cancellation
→ Charges and references never checked

The requirement said:
"A return is just a cancellation with money attached."

Why?

Treat a pacs.004 as what it is, a real payment in reverse: settled funds moving backward through the same chain, carrying its own charges and its own references. It applies when the beneficiary bank finds a closed or frozen account, a duplicate payment, or a wrong beneficiary after settlement. Its return chain element preserves the original chain so every intermediary knows its place, and returns deserve the same operational controls as outward payments.

A return is a payment in reverse.

BA Takeaway

Run every pacs.004 with the same controls as an outward payment: charges, references and chain included.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Return chain
→ Return charges
→ Original references

The real requirement is not "When do we act?"

It is "What evidence proves this return followed the original chain, with its charges accounted for?"

Have you treated a return as paperwork when it was really money moving?
takeaway: A return is a payment in reverse.

title: A EUR 130,000 payment went missing. The investigation started with a free-text email.
explain:
A EUR 130,000 payment goes missing and a customer complains.
The investigation starts with a free-text email to the correspondent, with no references.
Days pass, the case has no deadline, and the backlog grows.

Here is how that happens:

→ EUR 130,000 payment missing
→ Investigation opened with no SLA
→ Correspondent contacted by free-text email
→ Case drifts with no deadline

The requirement said:
"Investigations run on experience and instinct."

Why?

A payment investigation is a fixed sequence: intake and triage, identify the payment, verify the true status, check compliance, contact the correspondent, and resolve. Give every case type an SLA and an escalation matrix, because investigations without deadlines become backlogs. And contact the correspondent with structured queries and full references, never free-text emails that go nowhere.

Investigations run on rails, not instinct.

BA Takeaway

Run every investigation through the fixed sequence, with an SLA, an escalation matrix and structured correspondent queries.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Case SLA
→ Escalation matrix
→ Structured queries

The real requirement is not "When do we act?"

It is "What evidence proves this case is on track, with a deadline and an owner?"

Have you chased a missing payment with a free-text email that went nowhere?
takeaway: Investigations run on rails, not instinct.

title: EUR 250,000 held for three days on a name mismatch. The status said Pending, and the team read it as rejected.
explain:
A EUR 250,000 payment sits uncredited for three days.
The pacs.002 shows Pending, and the team treats it as a rejection.
The beneficiary bank is holding the payment, waiting for the name to be corrected.

Here is how that happens:

→ EUR 250,000 payment sent
→ pacs.002 shows Pending
→ Team reads Pending as rejected
→ Beneficiary bank holds the payment on a name mismatch

The requirement said:
"Pending means rejected."

Why?

A 250,000 euro payment sat uncredited for three days because the beneficiary bank flagged a name mismatch. A pacs.002 showing Pending means the beneficiary bank is holding the payment, not rejecting it, so open with an investigation query for the exact mismatch detail. Correct and verify the name and the bank applies the funds; if it cannot be resolved the payment returns via pacs.004, so validate beneficiary details at initiation, including confirmation of payee where the corridor supports it.

Pending is a hold, not a rejection.

BA Takeaway

Read Pending as a hold, ask for the exact mismatch detail, and validate beneficiary names at initiation.

Keep these controls separate:

→ pacs.002 Pending status
→ Name mismatch detail
→ Beneficiary validation

The real requirement is not "When do we act?"

It is "What evidence proves what the name mismatch actually is?"

Have you written off a payment that was only ever pending?
takeaway: Pending is a hold, not a rejection.

title: A EUR 2,000 collection was made by mistake. The team used one cancel button for all three stages.
explain:
A creditor realises a EUR 2,000 collection was made by mistake.
The team reaches for one generic cancel requirement.
The collection is already in the clearing flow, and the generic cancel does nothing.

Here is how that happens:

→ EUR 2,000 collection made by mistake
→ Creditor wants it stopped
→ Collection sits in the clearing flow
→ Generic cancel requirement applied

The requirement said:
"One cancel requirement covers every mistaken collection."

Why?

When a creditor realises a collection was made by mistake, the right mechanism depends on where the collection sits in its lifecycle. While it is warehoused with the creditor PSP and has not entered the inter-PSP flow, the creditor revokes it, and once it is in the clearing flow but before settlement, the creditor requests cancellation through the PSP or CSM process. After clearing and settlement, only a reversal can reimburse the debtor for the erroneous collection, and one generic cancel requirement cannot cover all three because the stage, initiator, mechanism and responsibilities differ, with refund the remaining step after settlement.

Stop a mistaken collection by its lifecycle stage.

BA Takeaway

Name the stage first, then choose revoke, cancel or reverse, and never write one generic cancel requirement.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Collection lifecycle stage
→ Revoke path
→ Cancel path
→ Reversal path

The real requirement is not "When do we act?"

It is "What evidence proves which stage this collection is in?"

Have you tried to cancel a collection that had already moved past cancelling?
takeaway: Stop a mistaken collection by its lifecycle stage.

title: A EUR 60,000 payment was processed, but by mid-morning there was still no credit. The customer called, and nobody could trace it.
explain:
A EUR 60,000 cross-border payment is processed.
By mid-morning the beneficiary still has no credit.
The customer calls, and the team has no live trace, so one query becomes hours of back-and-forth.

Here is how that happens:

→ EUR 60,000 payment processed
→ No credit by mid-morning
→ Customer query arrives
→ No live trace available

The requirement said:
"A processed payment can be found by asking around."

Why?

A processed cross-border payment can still show no credit by mid-morning because it may have failed silently, queued, stalled on missing details, or stopped for compliance checks, and without a live trace one customer query becomes hours of back-and-forth, reconciliation and investigation. Visibility comes from three elements working together: the UETR, ISO 20022 structured data, and connected systems and processes. A payment without a trace leaves a customer question unanswered, while a tracked payment reconciles faster, clears exceptions sooner, and avoids duplication, failed credits and manual rework.

No trace turns one question into an investigation.

BA Takeaway

Give every payment a live trace built on the UETR, structured ISO 20022 data and connected systems.

Keep these controls separate:

→ UETR trace
→ Structured data
→ Connected systems

The real requirement is not "When do we act?"

It is "What evidence proves where this payment sits right now?"

Have you answered a customer query with no trace to check?
takeaway: No trace turns one question into an investigation.

title: An instant payment of EUR 5,000 left the account at once. The beneficiary received nothing.
explain:
An instant payment of EUR 5,000 is debited at once.
The beneficiary receives nothing.
The team assumes it was rejected and the money is on its way back, but the payment is stuck, not rejected.

Here is how that happens:

→ EUR 5,000 instant payment sent
→ Debit lands immediately
→ Beneficiary receives nothing
→ Team assumes a rejection

The requirement said:
"A failed instant payment means the money comes straight back."

Why?

When an instant payment fails, the debit can land immediately while the beneficiary receives nothing, so the first task is to establish the cause: a timeout, an account issue, a technical problem, a compliance issue, or insufficient funds. Failed payments split into two kinds: genuinely rejected ones, where the money returns to the payer, and stuck ones, which need investigation, sometimes with the receiving bank helping to return the money. The same payment can even end differently in different countries, so the operative question is not only whether money left, but what the outcome is and where the money now sits.

Find the outcome first. Rejected and stuck are not the same.

BA Takeaway

Establish the outcome before telling the customer anything: rejected means the money returns, stuck means investigate.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Failure cause
→ Rejected outcome
→ Stuck outcome

The real requirement is not "When do we act?"

It is "What evidence proves whether this payment was rejected or is stuck?"

Have you told a customer the money was coming back when it was only stuck?
takeaway: Find the outcome first. Rejected and stuck are not the same.

title: 90 percent of a remittance file failed, and the repair queue could not cope
explain:
A remittance file worth EUR 480,000 arrived for processing.

90 percent of its transactions failed a banking control.

Operations sent them all to the repair queue, and the queue collapsed under the volume.

Here's how it happened:

→ File received with 200 transactions
→ 180 transactions fail a control
→ Every failed item goes to repair
→ Valid items sit unprocessed while the queue grows
→ The customer cannot tell what was processed, what was not, and what must be corrected

The requirement said:
"Send failed transactions to the repair queue."

Why?

Repair works when only a few items fail. At 90 percent failure the problem is the file, not the items, and a repair queue cannot fix a bad file one transaction at a time.

A repair queue is not a file correction process.

BA Takeaway

Size decides the route. Small files can send exceptions to repair while valid items continue. Large files need a threshold.

Keep these controls separate:

→ File-level threshold check
→ Item-level repair
→ Release of valid transactions

The real requirement isn't "Where do failed items go?"

It's "What evidence proves this file is safe to process at all?"

Have you seen a repair queue used to fix a file that should have been rejected?
takeaway: A repair queue is not a file correction process.

title: No pacs.002 after 20 seconds, EUR 5,000 gone, and the customer asked for it to be sent again
explain:
A customer sent a EUR 5,000 instant payment.

Twenty seconds passed. No pacs.002 arrived.

The account stood debited, the funds had left, and the customer asked for the payment to be sent again.

Here's how it happened:

→ EUR 5,000 SCT Inst payment sent
→ 20 second timeout passes, no pacs.002
→ Customer account debited, funds gone, credit unconfirmed
→ Customer asks to resend the payment
→ Resending would risk a duplicate EUR 5,000 payment

The assumption was:
"No confirmation means the payment failed, so send it again."

Why?

In SCT Inst, absence of a pacs.002 after the 20 second timeout leaves the payment in limbo. The debit is posted and the funds have left, but credit to the beneficiary stays unconfirmed. Resending would risk a duplicate, so the sender bank must instead issue a pacs.028 status request and let the recipient bank investigate.

No confirmation is not a failure. It is a question.

BA Takeaway

Never resend on a missing pacs.002. Issue a pacs.028 status request. That investigation either confirms the credit, closing the case, or confirms rejection, triggering an automatic refund and restoration of the account.

Keep these controls separate:

→ The debit, posted
→ The confirmation, missing
→ The resend, forbidden
→ The pacs.028 investigation
→ The refund, if rejection is confirmed

The real requirement isn't "Did the payment go through?"

It's "What evidence proves the payment's true state before we act?"

takeaway: No confirmation is not a failure. It is a question.

title: A EUR 100,000 payment was tracked to the wrong person, and tracking could not stop it
explain:
A EUR 100,000 payment was sent to the wrong beneficiary.

The team watched it on tracking, and it showed ACSC, credited, within 30 minutes.

They sent a stop message. It had no effect, because the money was already with the beneficiary.

Here's how it happened:

→ EUR 100,000 sent to the wrong beneficiary
→ Tracking shows the payment moving, then ACSC within 30 minutes
→ Team sends a stop message
→ Stop has no effect, the payment is already credited
→ Recovery now needs a Stop and Recall request

The assumption was:
"Tracking a payment means we can stop it."

Why?

Tracking only shows where a payment is, while stopping it prevents credit to the beneficiary, and the two must never be confused. Once credited, the bank needs a Stop and Recall request, routed by urgency: FAST, acknowledged within 2 hours when the payment is settled and credited; MEDIUM, answered within 12 hours when the beneficiary bank needs time to reach the beneficiary; and SLOW, answered within 72 hours when more time is needed. Delay steadily shrinks the chance of recovery.

Tracking shows. Recall recovers.

BA Takeaway

When a payment goes to the wrong beneficiary, check the status first. If it is credited, skip the stop and send the Stop and Recall at the right urgency. Speed decides whether a recall remains possible.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Tracking, which only shows location
→ The credit status, ACSC or not
→ The Stop and Recall request
→ The urgency queue: FAST, MEDIUM, SLOW

The real requirement isn't "Can we see the payment?"

It's "What evidence proves the payment is still stoppable, or that recall is the only route?"

takeaway: Tracking shows. Recall recovers.

title: A camt.055 arrived for a EUR 75,000 payment, and the team sent a camt.056 before asking where the payment sat
explain:
A camt.055 cancellation request arrived for a EUR 75,000 payment.

The team sent a camt.056 straight away.

The payment was future-dated and had not been released, so the whole interbank chase was unnecessary.

Here's how it happened:

→ camt.055 cancellation request arrives
→ Team sends camt.056 without checking the lifecycle
→ Payment was future-dated, warehoused, never released
→ It could have been cancelled before execution, internally
→ Interbank messages sent for a payment that never left the bank

The assumption was:
"A cancellation request means send a camt.056."

Why?

When a camt.055 arrives, do not assume a camt.056 should be sent straight away. The first question is where the original payment sits in its lifecycle. A future-dated or warehoused payment that has not been released may be cancelled before execution, a payment pending a compliance decision must be considered alongside that process, and a payment already processed by the debtor bank is no longer an internal decision. In a direct and cover model, each leg is controlled by a different party, so the pacs.008 leg and the pacs.009 COV leg may each need their own follow-up.

A cancellation request only asks. It does not guarantee.

BA Takeaway

Before any cancellation message, ask where the payment sits. Then act on that leg, and that leg only. If the cancellation fails, determine the appropriate return or investigation path.

Keep these controls separate:

→ The payment lifecycle position
→ The warehoused leg, cancellable internally
→ The compliance-pending leg
→ The processed leg, no longer internal
→ Each leg in a direct and cover model

The real requirement isn't "Did we send the cancellation?"

It's "What evidence proves where the payment sits before we act?"

title: Four messages, one recall, and a EUR 35,000 question no one could answer
explain:
A EUR 35,000 payment needed recalling.

The team had four messages in front of them: camt.055, camt.056, pacs.004 and camt.029.

They argued for an hour about which one was not used in the flow, and the payment waited.

Here's how it happened:

→ Customer cancellation request, camt.055
→ Interbank cancellation request, camt.056
→ Payment return, pacs.004
→ Resolution of investigation, camt.029
→ Team debates which message is not used in the flow
→ EUR 35,000 payment waits while the debate runs

The assumption was:
"The debate matters more than the journey."

Why?

It does not. The end-to-end recall journey runs through camt.055, camt.056, pacs.004 and camt.029, and connecting the four messages into one journey is the point of the exercise, not naming each message on its own. The question of which message is not used stays open, and guessing it does not move the money.

Connect the journey first. Debate second.

BA Takeaway

When a recall lands, run the journey first: request, interbank request, return, resolution. The poll question can wait. The customer's money cannot.

Keep these controls separate:

→ The customer request, camt.055
→ The interbank request, camt.056
→ The return, pacs.004
→ The resolution, camt.029
→ The open question, answered with evidence, not a guess

The real requirement isn't "Which message is not used?"

It's "What evidence proves each step of the journey ran?"

Have you seen a payment wait while a team debated the messages?
takeaway: Connect the journey first. Debate second.

title: Supplier paid twice, EUR 12,000 doubled
explain:
A supplier payment appears twice on the account statement for the same amount, to the same supplier, on the same day.
The supplier confirms receiving two credits.
EUR 12,000 has left the account twice.

Here's how that happens:

→ Payment submitted for EUR 12,000
→ Statement shows two debits, same amount, same day
→ Supplier confirms two credits received

The assumption was:
"Same amount, same day, so it must be one payment shown twice."

Two identical credits are two payments until the evidence says otherwise. Reconstruct both payments end to end from the same evidence set: channel timestamp, idempotency key and payload hash, gateway reference, payment engine reference, ledger posting reference and clearing acknowledgement. Comparing the two sets shows whether the duplicate came from a client retry, a gateway redelivery or a missing idempotency check, and each cause has a different fix.

Two identical credits are two payments until the evidence says otherwise.

BA Takeaway

Collect the full evidence set for each payment before deciding the cause. A client retry, a gateway redelivery and a missing idempotency check all look the same on a statement, and each one needs a different fix.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Idempotency key and payload hash
→ Gateway reference
→ Payment engine reference
→ Ledger posting reference
→ Clearing acknowledgement

The real requirement isn't "Was it paid twice?"

It's "What evidence proves which submission created the second payment?"

Have you ever found two identical credits and had to prove whether it was a retry or a redelivery?
takeaway: Comparing the two sets of evidence shows whether the duplicate came from a client retry, a gateway redelivery or a missing idempotency check.

title: New channel live, customers charged twice
explain:
A new corporate payment channel goes live.
Days later the operations team notices duplicate debits: several corporate customers charged twice for the same instruction, and a few suppliers paid twice.
The release passed testing. The duplicates are real.

Here's how that happens:

→ New channel released
→ Duplicate debits noticed across customers
→ Some suppliers paid twice for one instruction

The assumption was:
"The release passed testing, so duplicates cannot happen."

Testing passed, but the live path still created duplicates. Contain the failure first by confirming whether duplicates are still being created and, if so, stopping the affected path or routing it through a manual check. Then establish the affected population using stable identifiers rather than guesswork, matching on idempotency key, instruction reference, end-to-end identification, debtor, creditor, amount, currency and value date, and separate confirmed duplicates from suspected ones before remediating.

A duplicate is a control failure, not a display error.

BA Takeaway

Contain before you diagnose. Stop the path that is still creating duplicates, then build the affected population from stable identifiers, separate confirmed duplicates from suspected ones, and only then remediate.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Confirmed duplicates
→ Suspected duplicates
→ Remediation per case

The real requirement isn't "How many duplicates are there?"

It's "What evidence proves a payment is a confirmed duplicate, and is the path still creating more?"

Have you ever had to stop a live channel because it was still creating duplicates while you investigated?
takeaway: Establish the affected population using stable identifiers rather than guesswork, and separate confirmed duplicates from suspected ones before remediating.

steps.title: Contain the failure

title: Debited, rejected, and the EUR 20,000 must come back
explain:
The originator bank deducts EUR 20,000 from the customer for a payment.
The payment never reaches the beneficiary, because the clearing system rejected it.
The customer sees a deduction with no payment, and the money is sitting with the clearing system.

Here's how that happens:

→ Originator bank deducts EUR 20,000 from the customer
→ Clearing system rejects the payment
→ Clearing system holds the rejected funds
→ Return travels back to the originator bank
→ Originator bank credits the customer

The assumption was:
"A rejected payment returns itself."

The clearing system holds the funds it rejected, so the return starts there and travels back to the originator bank, which credits the customer. A rejection is not a return. Until the return message and the funds travel back, the customer has paid for nothing.

A rejection without a return leaves the customer paying for nothing.

BA Takeaway

Trace the return, not just the rejection. The funds sit with the clearing system that rejected them, the return starts there, and the customer is whole only when the originator bank credits the account.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Deduction from the customer
→ Rejection by the clearing system
→ Funds held by the clearing system
→ Return to the originator bank
→ Credit to the customer

The real requirement isn't "Was the payment rejected?"

It's "What evidence proves the rejected funds have travelled back to the customer?"

Have you ever had to explain to a customer that the payment was rejected, but the money had not come back yet?
takeaway: The customer sees a deduction with no payment, and the return is what makes the customer whole.

title: One misspelt name in field 50, EUR 30,000 sent back
explain:
An MT103 for EUR 30,000 is sent to pay a supplier.
The ordering customer name in field 50 is misspelt by one letter.
The payment comes back. The supplier is unpaid, and the ordering customer cannot understand why one letter stopped EUR 30,000.

Here's how that happens:

→ Name in field 50 is misspelt
→ Screening and reconciliation flag the name
→ MT103 returned to the originator bank

The assumption was:
"A small spelling error cannot stop a payment."

The misspelling matters because screening and reconciliation match on the name, and a name that does not match the account can look like a different party. The return is therefore a data-quality failure, not a funds failure, and it is fixed by correcting the name and resending.

A return over a name is a data failure, not a funds failure.

BA Takeaway

Check the name against the account before sending, not after the return. Screening matches on the name, and a name that does not match looks like a different party.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Field 50 name
→ Account holder name
→ Screening match
→ Reconciliation match

The real requirement isn't "Is the money there?"

It's "What evidence proves the name in field 50 matches the account holder?"

Have you ever had a payment returned over a single misspelt letter?
takeaway: The return is therefore a data-quality failure, not a funds failure, and it is fixed by correcting the name and resending.

title: Cancelled, recalled, disputed: three words, three different acts
explain:
A EUR 40,000 SEPA payment has gone wrong.
The team argues about whether to cancel it, recall it, or dispute it, as if the three words meant the same thing.
They do not, and picking the wrong one sends the wrong message.

Here's how that happens:

→ Payment has gone wrong
→ Is it settled or not?
→ Cancellation stops a payment before settlement
→ Recall requested with camt.056, answered with camt.029
→ Return made with pacs.004

The assumption was:
"Undoing a payment is one action."

In SEPA, a dispute, a cancellation, and a recall are three different actions. A recall is requested with a camt.056 and answered with a camt.029, a return is made with a pacs.004, and a cancellation stops a payment before it settles. The three are often confused because they all undo a payment, but they apply at different stages and they use different messages.

Cancellation, recall and return apply at different stages and use different messages.

BA Takeaway

Ask first whether the payment has settled. Before settlement, cancel it. After settlement, recall it with camt.056 and wait for the camt.029, and the return itself travels as pacs.004.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Cancellation before settlement
→ Recall with camt.056
→ Answer with camt.029
→ Return with pacs.004

The real requirement isn't "How do we undo it?"

It's "What evidence proves which stage the payment is at, and which message that stage needs?"

Have you ever sent a recall for a payment that should have been cancelled, or the other way round?

title: Five returns in six weeks over one wrong field
explain:
A payment sent to Australia was returned five times over six weeks.
Each time the note said the same thing: the beneficiary bank's SWIFT code had to appear in field 57A.
The code was right there in the message, in field 72 and in field 52A, where the receiving bank could see it.
It still came back, five times.

Here's how that happens:

→ Payment sent to Australia
→ SWIFT code placed in field 72 and 52A
→ Payment returned, code required in field 57A
→ Beneficiary bank taken over, code changed
→ New code used in field 57A, payment applied

The assumption was:
"If the receiving bank can see the code, the field does not matter."

The code had been placed in field 72 and in field 52A, where the receiving bank could see it, but that did not satisfy the validation: field 57A is the field the receiving bank reads to find the account with institution. The beneficiary bank had also been taken over and its SWIFT code had changed, so the sender had to use the new code in field 57A before the payment could be applied.

The right value in the wrong field is still wrong.

BA Takeaway

Put the code where the receiving bank reads it, and check the code is still current. Field 57A is the account with institution field, and a takeover can change the code without anyone telling the sender.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Field 57A, account with institution
→ Field 72, sender to receiver information
→ Field 52A, ordering institution
→ Current SWIFT code after takeover

The real requirement isn't "Is the code in the message?"

It's "What evidence proves the current code sits in the field the receiving bank reads?"

Have you ever had the same payment returned five times over one field?
takeaway: The beneficiary bank had also been taken over and its SWIFT code had changed, so the sender had to use the new code in field 57A before the payment could be applied.

title: Credited already? The recall is only a request
explain:
A EUR 18,000 payment has been credited to the wrong beneficiary.
The sender bank wants the money back.
It has no power to command it back. It can only ask.

Here's how that happens:

→ Sender bank issues camt.056
→ Beneficiary bank tests whether the funds are still available
→ camt.029 answers, accepted or rejected
→ pacs.004 moves the money only on acceptance

The assumption was:
"A recall commands the money back."

Once the beneficiary bank has credited the customer, the sender bank has no power to command the money back; it can only request it. The sender sends a camt.056 cancellation request, the beneficiary bank tests whether the funds are still available and answers with a camt.029, and a pacs.004 moves the money only on acceptance. A rejection leaves the sender with a commercial claim outside the payment rails, so the camt.056 must go out fast, while the funds are still there.

A recall is a request, not a command.

BA Takeaway

Send the camt.056 fast, while the funds are still there. The beneficiary bank tests availability, answers with camt.029, and the pacs.004 moves the money only on acceptance. A rejection leaves a commercial claim outside the rails.

Keep these controls separate:

→ camt.056 request
→ camt.029 answer
→ pacs.004 return on acceptance
→ Commercial claim on rejection

The real requirement isn't "Can we recall it?"

It's "What evidence proves the funds are still available, and how fast did we ask?"

Have you ever sent a recall a day too late, and found the funds already gone?
takeaway: A rejection leaves the sender with a commercial claim outside the payment rails, so the camt.056 must go out fast, while the funds are still there.

title: Duplicate payouts: 90 percent recovered, 10 percent still missing
explain:
A payout batch fires twice, and suppliers are paid double.
The team starts diagnosing the cause while the batch is still running.
More duplicates are being created while they investigate, and 10 percent of the duplicated value is still missing.

Here's how that happens:

→ Payout batch fires twice
→ Duplicates still being created
→ Recovery at 90 percent, 10 percent still missing

The assumption was:
"Diagnose first, contain later."

Duplicates demand containment before diagnosis: freeze the retry and payout batch so no more duplicates are created while the team investigates. Then identify the full population by reference or idempotency key, reverse the duplicates systematically, and track recovery until every case is closed. The cause here was a retry firing twice after a timeout through an idempotency gap, and the permanent fix is idempotency keys on every payout plus real-time reconciliation flagging double credits.

Contain first. A duplicate still being created is worse than one already made.

BA Takeaway

Freeze the retry and the payout batch first. Then identify the full population by reference or idempotency key, reverse systematically, track recovery to closure, and fix the idempotency gap so it cannot fire twice again.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Freeze the batch
→ Full population by reference or idempotency key
→ Systematic reversal
→ Recovery tracked to closure
→ Idempotency fix

The real requirement isn't "What caused it?"

It's "What evidence proves no more duplicates are being created, and every case is closed?"

Have you ever investigated a duplicate while the batch was still creating more of them?
takeaway: The cause here was a retry firing twice after a timeout through an idempotency gap, and the permanent fix is idempotency keys on every payout plus real-time reconciliation flagging double credits.

title: GBP 125,000 left. No trace, no rejection, no return.
explain:
A 125,000 pound international payment left the sender.
It never arrived.
No rejection, no return, no confirmation. The beneficiary is waiting, the sender is asking, and the payment has vanished from every screen that matters.

Here's how that happens:

→ Payment leaves the sender
→ No arrival, no rejection, no return
→ Beneficiary waiting, sender asking

The assumption was:
"No news means it failed. Send it again."

Before acting, prove what happened: pull the UETR, check the tracker for the last confirmed hop, and ask whether the money sits with an intermediary, in a compliance review, or stuck in a queue. Never re-send until the original is accounted for, because a duplicate is worse than a delay, and keep both sender and expectant beneficiary updated.

Never re-send until the original is accounted for. A duplicate is worse than a delay.

BA Takeaway

Prove first. Pull the UETR, find the last confirmed hop, and ask the three questions: intermediary, compliance review, or queue. Contact the intermediary with structured references, never a vague question, and update both sides while the uncertainty lasts.

Keep these controls separate:

→ UETR and last confirmed hop
→ Intermediary hold
→ Compliance review
→ Queue
→ Structured enquiry

The real requirement isn't "Did it fail?"

It's "What evidence proves where the original payment is right now?"

Have you ever had GBP 125,000 vanish with no trace, and had to prove what happened before anyone would act?
takeaway: Never re-send until the original is accounted for, because a duplicate is worse than a delay, and keep both sender and expectant beneficiary updated.

title: pacs.004 arrived. The debtor is still waiting.
explain:
A pacs.004 arrives, and the operations team credits the debtor at once.
The EUR 85,000 payment was a cover payment, a pacs.009, and the pacs.008 instruction was never rejected.
The debtor has been credited for a payment that was never returned, and the original instruction is still live.

Here's how that happens:

→ pacs.004 arrives
→ Team credits the debtor at once
→ Return relates to a rejected pacs.009 cover
→ pacs.008 instruction never rejected

The assumption was:
"A return means credit the debtor."

A pacs.004 only says a payment was returned, so crediting the debtor on receipt is an event-to-action shortcut that skips the questions that matter: what the return is for, who initiated it, whether the original was a pacs.008 or a pacs.009, why it was returned, and what happened to the original payment. When the pacs.004 relates to a rejected pacs.009 cover payment, the related pacs.008 cannot be assumed rejected, since the cover may have failed for lack of correspondent funds, wrong beneficiary correspondent or bank details, or a cover rejection for incorrect bank information.

A pacs.004 only says a payment was returned. It does not decide the debtor credit.

BA Takeaway

Investigate before crediting. Establish what the return is for, who initiated it, whether the original was a pacs.008 or a pacs.009, why it was returned, and the status of the original payment and any open exception. Only then choose between re-initiating the pacs.009, returning funds to the debtor, re-initiating the pacs.008, or another defined action.

Keep these controls separate:

→ What the return is for
→ Who initiated it
→ Original pacs.008 or pacs.009
→ Why it was returned
→ Status of the original payment

The real requirement isn't "Did a pacs.004 arrive?"

It's "What evidence proves what the return relates to, and what should happen to the original?"

Have you ever credited a debtor on a pacs.004, then found the original payment was never returned?
takeaway: A pacs.004 only says a payment was returned, so crediting the debtor on receipt is an event-to-action shortcut that skips the questions that matter.

title: Cancelling a SEPA payment: the right message each time
explain:
A customer asks to cancel a EUR 12,000 SEPA payment, and the team reaches for camt.056.
The payment is a direct debit, not a credit transfer.
The camt.056 goes nowhere, and the debit is collected anyway.

Here's how that happens:

→ Customer asks to cancel a SEPA payment
→ Is it a credit transfer, a direct debit, or a pain.008?
→ Wrong message sent, payment proceeds

The assumption was:
"One cancellation message fits every SEPA payment."

In the SEPA Credit Transfer scheme camt.056 is the message used to request cancellation of an SCT transaction. For SDD Core reversals the creditor bank sends pacs.007 against funds mistakenly debited. Corporations may also send camt.055 through their bank to cancel a pain.008: an unexecuted transaction is cancelled, while an executed one is reversed by the bank with pacs.007 instead.

The message depends on the scheme and on whether the payment has executed.

BA Takeaway

Ask two questions before sending anything: which scheme, and has the payment executed? SCT takes camt.056. SDD Core takes pacs.007. A pain.008 takes camt.055, and an executed one is reversed by the bank with pacs.007 instead.

Keep these controls separate:

→ SCT, camt.056
→ SDD Core, pacs.007
→ pain.008, camt.055
→ Executed or not

The real requirement isn't "How do we cancel it?"

It's "What evidence proves which scheme it is, and whether it has executed?"

Have you ever sent the right cancellation message to the wrong kind of payment?

explain:
EUR 25,000 was sent to a new beneficiary bank for the first time.
The customer was told it was sent.
Three days later, nothing had arrived.

Here is how that happens:

→ MT103 sent to the beneficiary bank
→ Receiving bank system refuses the message
→ No RMA exists for this sender
→ Sender receives no credit advice
→ Customer waits for money that never left

The assumption said:
"Send the MT103. The relationship paperwork can follow."

So the payment went out before anyone checked whether the receiving bank was authorised to accept it.

Why?

Before one bank can send an MT103 to another over SWIFT, the receiving bank must set up an RMA, a relationship management authorisation, for that sender. Without an RMA the receiving bank system will not accept the message at all.

No RMA, no message. No message, no payment.

An RMA is a precondition, not a formality to sort out afterwards.

BA Takeaway

An RMA is a precondition for the payment.

Keep these controls separate:

→ RMA in place for the receiving bank
→ MT103 sent and accepted
→ Credit advice received

Check the RMA before the first payment to any new bank, and confirm it again after a merger or a BIC change.

The real requirement is not "When do we send the MT103?"

It is "What evidence proves the receiving bank can accept our message?"

Have you seen a first payment fail because nobody checked the RMA?
takeaway: An RMA is a precondition, not paperwork to finish later. No RMA, no message, no payment.

explain:
EUR 12,000 was sent to pay a supplier invoice.
The IBAN was correct.
The money sat in suspense for a week.

Here is how that happens:

→ MT103 sent with field 59 showing IBAN and address
→ No beneficiary name anywhere in field 59
→ Beneficiary bank cannot confirm who the account belongs to
→ Payment held in suspense
→ Sender bank asked to supply the missing name

The assumption said:
"The IBAN is enough. The name is a nicety."

So the payment carried an account number and no identity, and the receiving bank had to choose between guessing and holding.

Why?

Field 59 is meant to identify the beneficiary. An MT103 can arrive showing only the IBAN and address, with no name at all, and then the beneficiary bank cannot confirm that the account belongs to the person the payment was meant for. It holds the payment and asks for confirmation instead of crediting it.

An account number is not an identity.

A correct IBAN with no name is a payment the bank cannot safely apply.

BA Takeaway

Field 59 must name the person the money is for.

Keep these controls separate:

→ IBAN valid and complete
→ Beneficiary name present in field 59
→ Name matched to the account before credit

Validate the name at instruction, not after the money is stuck.

The real requirement is not "Is the IBAN right?"

It is "What evidence proves this account belongs to the intended beneficiary?"

Have you seen a payment held because the name was missing?
takeaway: Field 59 must name the person the money is for. An account number is not an identity.

explain:
EUR 48,000 was paid against a supplier invoice.
The supplier was credited in full.
The supplier still chased the payment as unpaid.

Here is how that happens:

→ MT103 sent with field 70 carrying a 24-character reference
→ The /RFB/ reference is cut at 16 characters
→ Beneficiary credited the full EUR 48,000
→ Supplier reconciliation cannot match the truncated reference
→ Funds sit unapplied while the invoice shows overdue

The assumption said:
"Put the full reference in field 70. The system will carry it."

So a reference longer than the field allows was sent anyway, and the part that identified the invoice never arrived.

Why?

Field 70 carries remittance information, and the reference that follows /RFB/ is limited to 16 characters. A longer description must continue on the following lines of the field instead of stretching the reference, and a field 70 that repeats a code or overruns the limit is not a valid instruction.

Credited is not reconciled.

The money arrived. The meaning of the money did not.

BA Takeaway

A reference the receiver cannot read is a payment the supplier cannot find.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Reference fits the 16-character limit
→ Remittance detail continues on the next lines
→ Beneficiary confirms the invoice is matched

Validate reference length at instruction, before the MT103 leaves.

The real requirement is not "Did the money arrive?"

It is "What evidence proves the receiver matched it to the right invoice?"

explain:
EUR 60,000 was sent to a supplier through the usual corridor.
The payment was rejected downstream.
The intermediary named in the instruction had stopped serving that corridor months earlier.

Here is how that happens:

→ Payment instructed with Intermediary Agent 2 named
→ Routing trusts the stored intermediary data
→ Intermediary cannot serve the currency or the corridor
→ Payment rejected downstream
→ Repair starts, with no owner to fix the data

The assumption said:
"Reference data looks after itself."

So nobody owned the intermediary data, nobody validated it, and the same dead bank kept being named until a rejection exposed it.

Why?

Reference data without an owner decays. Intermediary Agent 2 quietly points payments at a bank that no longer serves the corridor, and the failure is unreadable at first, because message mapping, routing reference data and routing logic all look equally guilty.

Reference data without an owner decays.

The payment was right. The map it followed was out of date.

BA Takeaway

Every routing field needs a named owner and a validation rule.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Intermediary owner named
→ Validation rule against the corridor
→ Update process when a bank exits a corridor
→ Routing control that stops a stale intermediary

Leave any of the four out and the same bad intermediary keeps reappearing.

The real requirement is not "Who do we route through?"

It is "What evidence proves this intermediary still serves this corridor?"

Have you seen a payment die on an intermediary that had already left?
takeaway: Reference data without an owner decays. Every routing field needs a named owner and a validation rule.

explain:
EUR 90,000 was sent to settle a trade.
The purpose code field was left blank.
The beneficiary bank held the payment for compliance, and the trade could not settle.

Here is how that happens:

→ Customer sends the payment without a purpose code
→ Payment travels the chain without it
→ Beneficiary bank compliance needs the code
→ Payment held pending the missing detail
→ Trade settlement waits on a blank field

The assumption said:
"The customer can leave it blank. Someone downstream will fill it in."

So a code that was optional at the front and mandatory downstream had no owner, no enrichment source and no early validation.

Why?

A purpose code that is optional at the customer and mandatory downstream is a defect waiting for a payment. Enrichment needs a named owning source, and validation must happen early enough to catch a missing code before the payment reaches the system that needs it.

Optional at the front is not optional downstream.

The payment was complete at the front. It was incomplete where it mattered.

BA Takeaway

Name the system that needs the code, and validate before the payment travels.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Downstream system that needs the code, named
→ Enrichment owning source, named
→ Early validation before the payment travels
→ Repair behaviour, who fixes it and how fast

The real requirement is not "Can the customer leave it blank?"

It is "What evidence proves every downstream system has what it needs?"

Have you seen a payment held for a field nobody owned?
takeaway: Optional at the front is not optional downstream. Name the system that needs the code, and validate early.

explain:
A supplier payment went out at 2am by Faster Payments.
It was meant to arrive in seconds.
It arrived in the morning.

Here is how that happens:

→ Payment sent at 2am by Faster Payments
→ Faster Payments runs around the clock
→ Sending bank hits its liquidity limit
→ Payment queues until liquidity returns
→ Supplier paid in the morning, not in seconds

The assumption said:
"Faster Payments runs around the clock, so it always arrives in seconds."

So the team chose the rail for speed and never checked the liquidity behind it.

Why?

Faster Payments runs around the clock, but with liquidity limits. The scheme is always open, and the bank still needs the funds to settle. An urgent payment at 2am is fast only if the sending bank holds the liquidity to back it.

Around the clock is the scheme. Liquidity is the bank.

The rail was open all night. The money was not.

BA Takeaway

An urgent payment needs liquidity checked, not just the rail chosen.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Rail availability, around the clock
→ Sender liquidity, checked before sending
→ Queued payment, watched until release
→ Supplier promise, matched to the real arrival time

The real requirement is not "Which rail is fastest?"

It is "What evidence proves the funds are there to settle this payment now?"

Have you seen an instant payment wait until morning?
takeaway: Around the clock is the scheme. Liquidity is the bank. Check liquidity, not just the rail.
